_**The Bad Man**_ is a 1941 American Western film directed by Richard Thorpe and starring Wallace Beery and featuring Lionel Barrymore, Laraine Day and Ronald Reagan. The script was written by Wells Root from the 1920 Porter Emerson Browne play of the same name. The film is a remake of the 1923 silent version and the 1930 remake starring Walter Huston.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bad_Man_(1941_film)#cite_note-pryor-1)
The film is printed in a warm sepia tone, lending it a distinctive dusty, antique visual quality suited to its frontier setting.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bad_Man_(1941_film)#cite_note-catalog.afi.com-1-2)
Lionel Barrymore as Henry Jones
Wallace Beery as Pancho Lopez

Gil Jones is staying at his ranch in Mexico. His Uncle Henry, Jones, bound to a wheelchair, lives there. Unexpectedly, Gil's childhood sweetheart, Lucia comes to visit with her husband Morgan Pell, a New York businessman. Later that afternoon, the bandit Pancho Lopez raids the ranch, stealing all the cattle. During a firefight, Gil is wounded. Henry is upset over the loss of cattle because now they are broke; he also is worried over Lucia's concern for Gil. Later in the evening, Morgan privately tells Lucia that he has been happy in their marriage, but fears she may still love Gil. She promises Morgan that she will stay with him.
A month later, Lucia and Morgan come to visit Gil's ranch again. One day, Morgan goes into town on business. Gil and Lucia talk theoretically about love. Lucia reveals that she could never leave Morgan because he loves her so much. The banker Jasper Hardy arrives at the ranch with his daughter Angela; he is there to offer to buy the ranch, which is facing immediate foreclosure. Henry jokes that Gil should marry Angela.
Meanwhile, ranch hand "Red" Gidding walks around the ranch with Angela, with whom he has always been in love. Morgan returns from town and offers to buy the ranch for $20,000. Hardy is angry to have a competitor. Suspicious that these two men want a worthless ranch, Henry finally gets them to admit that the ranch may contain oil deposits. When Morgan raises his offer, Gil accepts at it and signs the sales agreement. Lucia is disappointed in Morgan. Gil then goes out to the barn.
Suddenly, Lopez and his gang arrive again and take everyone hostage, except for Gil, who is still in the barn. Lopez likes Henry and is attracted to Lucia, with whom he discusses love and freedom. The bandit immediately dislikes Morgan; he already hates Hardy because he is a banker. Lopez takes the mortgage document from Hardy and gives it to Gil. Unhappy about Gil selling the ranch, Henry tells Lopez about Hardy and Morgan conniving to get it. Then Lopez surprises everyone by saying the ranch has oil and he knows where to find it. He also claims that he is the rightful owner of the ranch.

Morgan and Hardy start a bidding war for the property, finally offering Lopez $200,000. However, he was lying about the oil; he only wanted to determine how much Hardy and Morgan were worth for ransom. Lopez and his men take everyone outside, but they encounter Gil, who is aiming a rifle at Lopez. However, the bandits manage to overcome Gil and Lopez orders him hanged, even though he is impressed with Gil's bravery.
As Gil is strung to a tree, Lopez suddenly recognizes him as the man who had saved his life five years before. He tells his men to cut Gil down and says that he wants to repay him by "changing the laws around here." Henry then explains to Lopez the unhappy romances at the ranch. Lopez uses some psychology to help Angela realize that she really loves Red.
Lopez then declares that he will kill Morgan, enabling Lucia and Gil to marry. Gil protest, saying that he doesn't want anyone hurt. When Lopez tells Morgan that he will be killed, he quickly offers to divorce Lucia. Lopez despises Morgan's cowardice and is unswayed by his further offer of money plus his wife. Lopez orders his man Pedro to take Morgan into the canyon to kill him. Lopez rides away with his men, saying that he will make Gil happy whether he wants it or not. In the canyon, Morgan tries to bribe Pedro without success. However, Pedro is distracted by the sounds of a firefight between the Lopez gang and "the policia," Morgan grabs Pedro's gun and shoots him dead.
Back inside the ranch house, Gil returns the mortgage to Hardy, who hastily leaves with Angela. Gil then comforts Lucia about her husband's pending murder. Morgan then arrives and sees the two of them together. He orders Lucia to leave the ranch with him, but she refuses. When he tries to draw his gun, Gil jumps on Morgan. During the scuffle, Lopez appears at the door and shoots Morgan to death. Lopez tells Gil about the murder of Pedro, and says "now everything is fixed."
When Lopez learns that Hardy has the mortgage again and the foreclosure sale is coming up quick, he offers to sell the stolen cattle to pay it off. Lopez then gives Henry's wheelchair a fast-paced tow to town to pay off the mortgage before the foreclosure sale.

In a contemporary review for _The New York Times_, critic Thomas M. Pryor called the _The Bad Man_ "the most static and loquacious Western we've encountered in a long time" and wrote: "You've seen 'The Bad Man' before, at least twice under its rightful title and goodness knows how many times under an assortment of aliases. ... Metro's mistake in this instance is that it stuck too close to the old Porter Emerson Browne play—so close that the film is practically a carbon copy of a three-act play in two scenes. Except for a Keystone ending, most of the action is confined to the living room of a ranch hard by the Rio Grande. As a consequence the actors just talk on and on, and what they have to say is, unfortunately, uninteresting."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bad_Man_(1941_film)#cite_note-pryor-1)

_**The Bad Man**_ is a 1941 American Western film directed by Richard Thorpe and starring Wallace Beery and featuring Lionel Barrymore, Laraine Day and Ronald Reagan. The script was written by Wells Root from the 1920 Porter Emerson Browne play of the same name. The film is a remake of the 1923 silent version and the 1930 remake starring Walter Huston.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bad_Man_(1941_film)#cite_note-pryor-1)
The film is printed in a warm sepia tone, lending it a distinctive dusty, antique visual quality suited to its frontier setting.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bad_Man_(1941_film)#cite_note-catalog.afi.com-1-2)

texts.1:
Gil Jones is staying at his ranch in Mexico. His Uncle Henry, Jones, bound to a wheelchair, lives there. Unexpectedly, Gil's childhood sweetheart, Lucia comes to visit with her husband Morgan Pell, a New York businessman. Later that afternoon, the bandit Pancho Lopez raids the ranch, stealing all the cattle. During a firefight, Gil is wounded. Henry is upset over the loss of cattle because now they are broke; he also is worried over Lucia's concern for Gil. Later in the evening, Morgan privately tells Lucia that he has been happy in their marriage, but fears she may still love Gil. She promises Morgan that she will stay with him.
A month later, Lucia and Morgan come to visit Gil's ranch again. One day, Morgan goes into town on business. Gil and Lucia talk theoretically about love. Lucia reveals that she could never leave Morgan because he loves her so much. The banker Jasper Hardy arrives at the ranch with his daughter Angela; he is there to offer to buy the ranch, which is facing immediate foreclosure. Henry jokes that Gil should marry Angela.
Meanwhile, ranch hand "Red" Gidding walks around the ranch with Angela, with whom he has always been in love. Morgan returns from town and offers to buy the ranch for $20,000. Hardy is angry to have a competitor. Suspicious that these two men want a worthless ranch, Henry finally gets them to admit that the ranch may contain oil deposits. When Morgan raises his offer, Gil accepts at it and signs the sales agreement. Lucia is disappointed in Morgan. Gil then goes out to the barn.
Suddenly, Lopez and his gang arrive again and take everyone hostage, except for Gil, who is still in the barn. Lopez likes Henry and is attracted to Lucia, with whom he discusses love and freedom. The bandit immediately dislikes Morgan; he already hates Hardy because he is a banker. Lopez takes the mortgage document from Hardy and gives it to Gil. Unhappy about Gil selling the ranch, Henry tells Lopez about Hardy and Morgan conniving to get it. Then Lopez surprises everyone by saying the ranch has oil and he knows where to find it. He also claims that he is the rightful owner of the ranch.
texts.2:
Morgan and Hardy start a bidding war for the property, finally offering Lopez $200,000. However, he was lying about the oil; he only wanted to determine how much Hardy and Morgan were worth for ransom. Lopez and his men take everyone outside, but they encounter Gil, who is aiming a rifle at Lopez. However, the bandits manage to overcome Gil and Lopez orders him hanged, even though he is impressed with Gil's bravery.
As Gil is strung to a tree, Lopez suddenly recognizes him as the man who had saved his life five years before. He tells his men to cut Gil down and says that he wants to repay him by "changing the laws around here." Henry then explains to Lopez the unhappy romances at the ranch. Lopez uses some psychology to help Angela realize that she really loves Red.
Lopez then declares that he will kill Morgan, enabling Lucia and Gil to marry. Gil protest, saying that he doesn't want anyone hurt. When Lopez tells Morgan that he will be killed, he quickly offers to divorce Lucia. Lopez despises Morgan's cowardice and is unswayed by his further offer of money plus his wife. Lopez orders his man Pedro to take Morgan into the canyon to kill him. Lopez rides away with his men, saying that he will make Gil happy whether he wants it or not. In the canyon, Morgan tries to bribe Pedro without success. However, Pedro is distracted by the sounds of a firefight between the Lopez gang and "the policia," Morgan grabs Pedro's gun and shoots him dead.
Back inside the ranch house, Gil returns the mortgage to Hardy, who hastily leaves with Angela. Gil then comforts Lucia about her husband's pending murder. Morgan then arrives and sees the two of them together. He orders Lucia to leave the ranch with him, but she refuses. When he tries to draw his gun, Gil jumps on Morgan. During the scuffle, Lopez appears at the door and shoots Morgan to death. Lopez tells Gil about the murder of Pedro, and says "now everything is fixed."
When Lopez learns that Hardy has the mortgage again and the foreclosure sale is coming up quick, he offers to sell the stolen cattle to pay it off. Lopez then gives Henry's wheelchair a fast-paced tow to town to pay off the mortgage before the foreclosure sale.

Metro's mistake in this instance is that it stuck too close to the old Porter Emerson Browne play—so close that the film is practically a carbon copy of a three-act play in two scenes. Except for a Keystone ending, most of the action is confined to the living room of a ranch hard by the Rio Grande. As a consequence the actors just talk on and on, and what they have to say is, unfortunately, uninteresting."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bad_Man_(1941_film)#cite_note-pryor-1)

_**The Bad Man**_ is a 1941 American Western film directed by Richard Thorpe and starring Wallace Beery and featuring Lionel Barrymore, Laraine Day and Ronald Reagan. The script was written by Wells Root from the 1920 Porter Emerson Browne play of the same name. The film is a remake of the 1923 silent version and the 1930 remake starring Walter Huston.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bad_Man_(1941_film)#cite_note-pryor-1)
The film is printed in a warm sepia tone, lending it a distinctive dusty, antique visual quality suited to its frontier setting.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bad_Man_(1941_film)#cite_note-catalog.afi.com-1-2)
Lionel Barrymore as Henry Jones
Wallace Beery as Pancho Lopez

Gil Jones is staying at his ranch in Mexico. His Uncle Henry, Jones, bound to a wheelchair, lives there. Unexpectedly, Gil's childhood sweetheart, Lucia comes to visit with her husband Morgan Pell, a New York businessman. Later that afternoon, the bandit Pancho Lopez raids the ranch, stealing all the cattle. During a firefight, Gil is wounded. Henry is upset over the loss of cattle because now they are broke; he also is worried over Lucia's concern for Gil. Later in the evening, Morgan privately tells Lucia that he has been happy in their marriage, but fears she may still love Gil. She promises Morgan that she will stay with him.
A month later, Lucia and Morgan come to visit Gil's ranch again. One day, Morgan goes into town on business. Gil and Lucia talk theoretically about love. Lucia reveals that she could never leave Morgan because he loves her so much. The banker Jasper Hardy arrives at the ranch with his daughter Angela; he is there to offer to buy the ranch, which is facing immediate foreclosure. Henry jokes that Gil should marry Angela.
Meanwhile, ranch hand "Red" Gidding walks around the ranch with Angela, with whom he has always been in love. Morgan returns from town and offers to buy the ranch for $20,000. Hardy is angry to have a competitor. Suspicious that these two men want a worthless ranch, Henry finally gets them to admit that the ranch may contain oil deposits. When Morgan raises his offer, Gil accepts at it and signs the sales agreement. Lucia is disappointed in Morgan. Gil then goes out to the barn.
Suddenly, Lopez and his gang arrive again and take everyone hostage, except for Gil, who is still in the barn. Lopez likes Henry and is attracted to Lucia, with whom he discusses love and freedom. The bandit immediately dislikes Morgan; he already hates Hardy because he is a banker. Lopez takes the mortgage document from Hardy and gives it to Gil. Unhappy about Gil selling the ranch, Henry tells Lopez about Hardy and Morgan conniving to get it. Then Lopez surprises everyone by saying the ranch has oil and he knows where to find it. He also claims that he is the rightful owner of the ranch.

Morgan and Hardy start a bidding war for the property, finally offering Lopez $200,000. However, he was lying about the oil; he only wanted to determine how much Hardy and Morgan were worth for ransom. Lopez and his men take everyone outside, but they encounter Gil, who is aiming a rifle at Lopez. However, the bandits manage to overcome Gil and Lopez orders him hanged, even though he is impressed with Gil's bravery.
As Gil is strung to a tree, Lopez suddenly recognizes him as the man who had saved his life five years before. He tells his men to cut Gil down and says that he wants to repay him by "changing the laws around here." Henry then explains to Lopez the unhappy romances at the ranch. Lopez uses some psychology to help Angela realize that she really loves Red.
Lopez then declares that he will kill Morgan, enabling Lucia and Gil to marry. Gil protest, saying that he doesn't want anyone hurt. When Lopez tells Morgan that he will be killed, he quickly offers to divorce Lucia. Lopez despises Morgan's cowardice and is unswayed by his further offer of money plus his wife. Lopez orders his man Pedro to take Morgan into the canyon to kill him. Lopez rides away with his men, saying that he will make Gil happy whether he wants it or not. In the canyon, Morgan tries to bribe Pedro without success. However, Pedro is distracted by the sounds of a firefight between the Lopez gang and "the policia," Morgan grabs Pedro's gun and shoots him dead.
Back inside the ranch house, Gil returns the mortgage to Hardy, who hastily leaves with Angela. Gil then comforts Lucia about her husband's pending murder. # The Bad Man (1941, directed by Richard Thorpe)
Posted on March 1, 2025 by Jedadiah Leland
Gil Jones (Ronald Reagan) lives on a ranch with his cantankerous uncle, Henry (Lionel Barrymore). After their cattle are stolen by the notorious bandit Pancho Lopez (Wallace Beery), Gil and Henry are faced with the prospect of losing their ranch. Banker Jasper Hardy (Henry Travers) wants to foreclose on Henry and take over the ranch but a businessman named Morgan Pell (Tom Conway) shows up and offers to pay the then-huge sum of $20,000 for the land. Accompanying Morgan is his wife, Lucia (Laraine Day). Lucia was Gil’s childhood love and Morgan fears that Lucia still loves Gil more than him. Also in the mix is Gil’s comic relief best friend (Chill Wills), who has a crush on Hardy’s daughter (Nydia Westman). Negotiations are interrupted when the flamboyant Lopez and his men return to the ranch and take everyone, but Gil, hostage.
This sepia-toned film is based on a stage play, one that had already been filmed twice. It was Ronald Reagan’s first film for MGM and, when Reagan was running for President, he quipped that if he could survive acting opposite Wallace Beery and Lionel Barrymore than he could survive negotiating with Leonid Brezhnev. The role of Gil is a typical Ronald Reagan role. He’s good-natured and dependable and a little boring. Because he once saved Lopez’s life, Lopez is willing to help him out with his problems. Reagan is not bad in the role but he is overshadowed by Barrymore and Beery, two veteran actors who chew the scenery with gusto here. Berry speaks in an exaggerated and not at all convincing Mexican accent while Barrymore bellows all of his lines. Gil has so many different people yelling at him that it’s impossible not to feel sorry for him. Morgan has ulterior motives for offering to buy the land and Tom Conway is a convincing villain. Lopez helps out Gil and her uncle, saving not only their land but also plotting to bring Gil and Lucia back together. It’s a stage bound mix of drama and comedy that doesn’t really work, though Beery and Barrymore are amusing and Ronald Reagan shows why he was cast in so many best friend roles.

# The Bad Man (1941, directed by Richard Thorpe)
Whether you’ll enjoy it will probably depend on how you feel about the cast because they’re really the only reason to watch. If you’re a fan of Barrymore, Beery, or Reagan the film might work for you. If you’re not, this stagey 70-minute western is probably not for you.

# The Bad Man (1941, directed by Richard Thorpe)
Posted on March 1, 2025 by Jedadiah Leland
Gil Jones (Ronald Reagan) lives on a ranch with his cantankerous uncle, Henry (Lionel Barrymore). After their cattle are stolen by the notorious bandit Pancho Lopez (Wallace Beery), Gil and Henry are faced with the prospect of losing their ranch. Banker Jasper Hardy (Henry Travers) wants to foreclose on Henry and take over the ranch but a businessman named Morgan Pell (Tom Conway) shows up and offers to pay the then-huge sum of $20,000 for the land. Accompanying Morgan is his wife, Lucia (Laraine Day). Lucia was Gil’s childhood love and Morgan fears that Lucia still loves Gil more than him. Also in the mix is Gil’s comic relief best friend (Chill Wills), who has a crush on Hardy’s daughter (Nydia Westman). Negotiations are interrupted when the flamboyant Lopez and his men return to the ranch and take everyone, but Gil, hostage.
This sepia-toned film is based on a stage play, one that had already been filmed twice. It was Ronald Reagan’s first film for MGM and, when Reagan was running for President, he quipped that if he could survive acting opposite Wallace Beery and Lionel Barrymore than he could survive negotiating with Leonid Brezhnev. The role of Gil is a typical Ronald Reagan role. He’s good-natured and dependable and a little boring. Because he once saved Lopez’s life, Lopez is willing to help him out with his problems. Reagan is not bad in the role but he is overshadowed by Barrymore and Beery, two veteran actors who chew the scenery with gusto here. Berry speaks in an exaggerated and not at all convincing Mexican accent while Barrymore bellows all of his lines. Gil has so many different people yelling at him that it’s impossible not to feel sorry for him. Morgan has ulterior motives for offering to buy the land and Tom Conway is a convincing villain. Lopez helps out Gil and her uncle, saving not only their land but also plotting to bring Gil and Lucia back together. It’s a stage bound mix of drama and comedy that doesn’t really work, though Beery and Barrymore are amusing and Ronald Reagan shows why he was cast in so many best friend roles.

# The Bad Man (1941, directed by Richard Thorpe)
Posted on March 1, 2025 by Jedadiah Leland
Gil Jones (Ronald Reagan) lives on a ranch with his cantankerous uncle, Henry (Lionel Barrymore). After their cattle are stolen by the notorious bandit Pancho Lopez (Wallace Beery), Gil and Henry are faced with the prospect of losing their ranch. Banker Jasper Hardy (Henry Travers) wants to foreclose on Henry and take over the ranch but a businessman named Morgan Pell (Tom Conway) shows up and offers to pay the then-huge sum of $20,000 for the land. Accompanying Morgan is his wife, Lucia (Laraine Day). Lucia was Gil’s childhood love and Morgan fears that Lucia still loves Gil more than him. Also in the mix is Gil’s comic relief best friend (Chill Wills), who has a crush on Hardy’s daughter (Nydia Westman). Negotiations are interrupted when the flamboyant Lopez and his men return to the ranch and take everyone, but Gil, hostage.
This sepia-toned film is based on a stage play, one that had already been filmed twice. It was Ronald Reagan’s first film for MGM and, when Reagan was running for President, he quipped that if he could survive acting opposite Wallace Beery and Lionel Barrymore than he could survive negotiating with Leonid Brezhnev. The role of Gil is a typical Ronald Reagan role. He’s good-natured and dependable and a little boring. Because he once saved Lopez’s life, Lopez is willing to help him out with his problems. Reagan is not bad in the role but he is overshadowed by Barrymore and Beery, two veteran actors who chew the scenery with gusto here. Berry speaks in an exaggerated and not at all convincing Mexican accent while Barrymore bellows all of his lines. Gil has so many different people yelling at him that it’s impossible not to feel sorry for him. Morgan has ulterior motives for offering to buy the land and Tom Conway is a convincing villain. Lopez helps out Gil and her uncle, saving not only their land but also plotting to bring Gil and Lucia back together. It’s a stage bound mix of drama and comedy that doesn’t really work, though Beery and Barrymore are amusing and Ronald Reagan shows why he was cast in so many best friend roles.

# The Bad Man (1941, directed by Richard Thorpe)
Whether you’ll enjoy it will probably depend on how you feel about the cast because they’re really the only reason to watch. If you’re a fan of Barrymore, Beery, or Reagan the film might work for you. If you’re not, this stagey 70-minute western is probably not for you.
